 Rain brings relief to Indonesian city choked by wildfire haze 
 Palangkaraya residents and firefighters celebrate, but weather agency warns dry spell could return 
 October 29, 2026 01:01 p.m

 PALANGKARAYA: Residents and firefighters in an Indonesian city shrouded for months in toxic haze from wildfires rushed outside to dance and chant as rain this week brought a welcome respite.
 Intermittent rain has been falling in Palangkaraya, the capital of Central Kalimantan province on Indonesian Borneo, where devastating wildfires have raged since August. On Wednesday night, exhausted volunteer firefighters jumped in puddles and kissed the ground as another downpour came. “We were overjoyed; every one of us volunteers was so happy that we prostrated ourselves in gratitude. Praise be to God that there was finally rain,” firefighter Lukman El Hakim told AFP.
 More than 11,000 people have been treated for respiratory infections in Palangkaraya during the crisis. The city’s air quality index hit 4,000 this month, its worst ever reading and more than 13 times the environment ministry’s “hazardous” threshold. Resident Muhammad Jihan Alwi, 23, used the break to go jogging outdoors for the first time in months. “Of course I’m happy to be out jogging again, breathing in fresh air that’s better than yesterday,” he said.
 But the BMKG climatology agency said dry weather would continue to dominate for a while, with more fires possible. “Although still in the ‘unhealthy’ category, there is now a downward trend compared with a week ago,” BMKG official Tri Handoko Seto said of PM2.5 levels, warning of “the possibility of another dry period before we fully enter the peak of the rainy season”. The disaster agency BNPB said it was operating 61 planes and helicopters for cloud seeding and water bombing in six provinces, and that its cloud seeding had encouraged recent rain in Central Kalimantan, South Kalimantan and South Sumatra.
 At least 11 people have died fighting the fires, most recently a 45-year-old forest ranger killed by a falling tree in North Toraja, South Sulawesi, on Wednesday. National police chief detective Asep Safrudin said 245 individuals and 20 corporations have been named as suspects over the fires and could face jail and heavy fines.
 The fires have burned more than 1.9 million hectares in the nine months to September, according to deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas, sending haze as far as Malaysia, Singapore, the Philippines and East Timor. Experts blame them largely on slash-and-burn land clearing, often by timber, palm oil and mining companies. — AFP
